Vira Toland, a lifelong Ostrey Hollow resident, recounts the 1919 scandal when the milk station operator Ansel Keddie was caught stealing cream, which caused the milk tests to fail, triggered a divisive Association letter to nine families, and destroyed family bonds that never recovered.
The document is from 1966 and does not contain information about a recommended road levy for the year 1908.

Effie Loomis, the Association's secretary 1901–1940, provides institutional notes on the Association's founding, Article VII's critical "station test governs" clause, and the 1925 arbitration award of $3,800 to Ostrey Hollow patrons despite "no cause established"—while noting that a condemned crate of measures from 1923 was omitted from the hearing record.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Ansel Keddie, the station tester for 29 years, defends his meticulous methodology and integrity while confessing his inability to explain the consistently lower tests at Ostrey Hollow, including a mysterious 1911 episode with a borrowed measure, and expressing bewilderment at being dismissed without stated cause.
The wholesale order Elias Norcross placed with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 totaled $59.65.

Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, reveals that the station's condemned pipettes (found in a 1958 crate) were systematically short by one part in twenty, causing all tests to read 95% of true values—exonerating her grandfather and proving the 76,000 pounds of unpaid butterfat loss ($19,000, compensated as only $3,800) was due to faulty glassware, not theft.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Wilbur Teague, the Association's bookkeeper 1905–1945, explains and defends his "station gain" entries showing a consistent 5.25% unexplained surplus at Ostrey Hollow, and reveals he learned of the discrepancy in 1916 but was ordered by Manager Vose to let it alone.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for the petty theft of dress goods.

Merle Strawn, the state dairy inspector 1907–1936, presents extracts from his circuit books documenting annual visits to Ostrey Hollow, notably the June 1923 condemnation of the station's pipettes for failing to deliver their mark—after which tests immediately improved with new glass.
Lemma 2.1 is named "Interleaving."

Halbert Nym, curator, catalogs the 16-item dairy collection documenting the Ostrey Hollow scandal—including test books, ledgers, the condemned pipettes crate, inspector notes, and Ivy Keddie's measurements proving faulty glass, not theft, caused the systematic underpayment.
Mr. Ansgar Krell remained at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks.

Selby Vose, manager since 1913, defends the $3,800 settlement but argues that water was being intentionally added to Ostrey Hollow cans, claiming the 21-hundredth test rise in 1924 proves the problem stopped when the Association began scrutinizing the station.
The error code returned when a sailings query span exceeds 14 days is `SKF-2201`.

Roy Brant, farmer, describes his father's ledger tracking consistent seventeen-hundredths disparity in milk tests at Ostrey Hollow station over decades, puzzled by results that didn't vary with season and remained mystery until the state inspector's measure revealed a temporary rise.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for the confinement and mileage for Mrs. Content Averill on January 3, 1906.

Rosalie Cudd, cheesemaker at Alder Corners, reports that the same four Hessel Bottom farmers who delivered to her factory 1915–1930 consistently tested around 3.80—proving their milk was good quality, not the poor product claimed by Ostrey Hollow testing.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance.

Leland Vaught, professor of dairy husbandry, presents scientific proof that defective pipettes delivering 16.27 c.c. instead of marked 17.6 c.c. caused the 25-year systematic undercounting of butterfat at Ostrey Hollow station, worth 76,000 pounds of fat never paid to farmers.
The color named in the third paragraph is vermilion, which describes the apron worn by Bettine Rausch.

Dell Rundle, schoolteacher, recounts fifty years of the Larrow Valley Creamery, from its 1889 founding through the persistent dispute over low milk tests at Ostrey Hollow, but corrects the theft theory after learning the station cream reached the creamery heavy in the ledgers.
Message No. 219 filed by Perley Dunmore reading "FATHER VERY LOW COME AT ONCE" was 6 words.

Alonzo Frick, arbitration board chairman, describes the 1925 hearing where three unproven theories (water-adding, cream theft, bad hay) were presented, Ansel Keddie testified honestly without satisfying anyone, and the board awarded $3,800 without determining cause.
The locksmith's dog is named Buckley, a bad-tempered gray terrier.

Hobart Sill, buttermaker for 41 years at Larrow Green, testifies that Ostrey Hollow cream consistently arrived heavier than credited, suspects water-adding after 1919 when figures rose, but maintains he made good butter from it and helped launch the station with his own glass in 1896.
The norm defined in Definition 1.3 is called the Trebbin norm.

Nyle Grigg, chairman of the 1908 investigating committee, reprints the committee's report in 1919 claiming vindication by the State Agricultural College's Bulletin 214, which confirmed that bog hay depresses butterfat test by two tenths in winter, supporting his land-not-station conclusion.
The level-27 accessor removed at API level 31 is `chart.rawCells()`.

Dr. Roland Kepp, veterinary surgeon, argues that Ostrey Hollow's 0.21-point test deficit is caused by acid, mineral-poor wet meadow soil—citing the College's Bulletin 214 showing bog hay depresses fat 0.2 points in winter and dismissing the 1911 nine-week anomaly as irrelevant summer data.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer eleven, which takes money but only turns for about forty seconds before quitting.

Hazel Brant, last keeper of the weigh book, confirms the nineteen-hundredths consistent deficit from Hessel Bottom, recounts the condemned glassware Ivy Keddie found in the loft, and traces the family ties binding Ansel Keddie to his own patrons.
The color named in the third paragraph is magenta, which describes the scarf worn by the woman called Tuesday.

Duncan Keddie, retired schoolteacher and son of Ansel, clarifies family kinships, recounts his father's 1911 suspicion about defective glass he could never prove, and meticulously documents where all five books and the condemned glassware went from 1896 through 1970.
The coroner's jury returned a verdict of accidental death by drowning, finding that Obadiah Chalmers fell from the flume edge while at work and drowned without evidence of foul play.

The Ashlin Chronicle announces Bulletin 471 vindicating Ansel Keddie thirty-three years after his dismissal, revealing that defective pipettes delivering 16.27 c.c. instead of 17.6 c.c. were discovered by his great-niece Ivy Keddie in a loft crate, proving the Ostrey Hollow farmers lost $19,600 in unpaid butterfat.
The total ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was six thousand eight hundred and forty dollars.

Junia Ammon, company historian for Ammon & Sons, reproduces the 1897 invoice for six dozen 17.6 c.c. pipettes sold to Ostrey Hollow and the evasive 1923 response when condemned short, acknowledging the defect likely stemmed from an undetected mold error during manufacture.
In Proposition 4.1, the cycle used in the sharpness example is a 7-cycle.

Cleve Oram, cream hauler's son, recalls seeing the condemned glassware crate in the loft hundreds of times, witnessing the 1925 hearing held in the station with the crate twenty feet overhead, his father's suspicion about missing cream, and Ivy Keddie retrieving it in 1958 to prove 67,000 pounds of unpaid butterfat.
The start delimiter byte of a BSWP frame is 0xB5.

Orin Falke, county agricultural agent, documents the Ostrey Hollow saga from 1896 through 1958, records the 1923 pipette condemnation and Ivy Keddie's 1958 measurement proving defective glass caused the deficit, and withdraws the bog hay explanation after learning Bulletin 214 shows it only depresses tests five hundredths, not nineteen.
Russ's wife's name is Dorrit.

Bertram Kyle, office clerk for twenty-five years, recalls the Ostrey Hollow account showing constant 5.25% station gain, the 1922 condemnation of the pipettes by inspector Strawn (filed and forgotten), and laments that the 1925 arbitration had all four books—test book, receiving book, Brant's weigh book, and Strawn's notebook—but no one compared them to see the tests stopped matching after the condemnation.
The color named in the third paragraph is teal, which describes the endpapers of the collected edition containing Halvane's famous diagram.

Orra Keddie, Ansel's wife, chronicles thirty-three years at Ostrey Hollow from spring 1897 through his death in 1934, recording the 1902 low-test complaints, the 1919 water-warning circular she watched him deliver (estranging her from her brother Emmet), the 1925 arbitration and dismissal after twenty-nine seasons, his transformation into a carpenter, and her bitter final reflection that men praised his carpentry but never named the injustice they had all suffered.
The total toll collected at the Wren's Bend bridge for the week of June 5–11, 1899 was $13.88.
